Triggers.value: Someone getting emotionally close to me

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion

Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel intense shame

Negative Appraisals.value: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: 'Explosion or bang sounds' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of chronic physical abuse by a romantic partner unless there is additional history not represented elsewhere. The rest of the profile centers on interpersonal/home-based threat, emotional closeness, family comments, shame, weakness, and hypervigilance for someone entering the home. An explosion-specific trigger pulls toward a very different trauma context and is not supported by the memory, threat, or appraisal items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm as a distraction strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly supported by the rest of the selected items. The maladaptive strategy set otherwise reflects avoidance and conflict-generation, while the connected nodes emphasize home intrusion vigilance, bodily reenactment, shame, weakness, and loss of trust. Because Maladaptive Strategies is strongly linked to Triggers and somewhat to Threat/Negative Appraisals here, a severe self-injurious coping item stands out as insufficiently integrated with the rest of the formulation and item pattern.

issues.item: Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
issues.explanation: 'Seeking Conflict' is hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile. The patient's trauma is intimate partner physical abuse, and the other nodes describe hypervigilance, shame, weakness, loss of trust, and avoidance. Deliberately creating interpersonal conflict is a marked shift in style that is not supported by the accompanying threat, memory, appraisal, or trigger items, making this maladaptive strategy clinically incoherent in this profile.

vignette:
María had been raised to believe that a home should be a place of order, privacy, and mutual respect, and for much of her adult life she had tried to build exactly that. Now 74, married, and long retired from her work as a pharmacist, she came to treatment describing a life that had narrowed in quiet ways over many years. The traumatic period she identified dated back to an earlier romantic relationship, when she was physically abused by a partner who could become frighteningly violent without warning. She did not speak about that history in sweeping terms; instead, she described it as a series of sharp, isolated moments that still returned to her with the force of the original scene. She remembered a door slamming so hard it seemed to split the air, the sound of someone entering too quickly, the sudden sense that there was nowhere to turn, and then the humiliating awareness of her own body being trapped in a position she had not chosen. When she recalled it, she did not experience the memory as a smooth narrative. It came to her in flashes, almost like separate photographs: one instant of the doorway, another of the room, another of herself frozen in place. She said that when the memory surfaced, she felt intense shame, as if she were seeing not only what happened to her but what it said about her.

Over time, María found herself watching her body with discomfort. She avoided looking closely at herself, including in mirrors or while dressing, and she described a growing reluctance to pay attention to bodily sensations at all. Certain feelings were just as hard to tolerate. If she sensed anger, sadness, or fear rising, she tried to shut it down quickly, telling herself she could not afford to let herself go there. She also began to avoid other people, not in a dramatic way but in a shrinking pattern of declining visits, ending conversations early, and keeping interaction brief. Even in marriage, she preferred distance when closeness felt emotionally demanding, and she noticed that when someone tried to become more emotionally close to her, she would tense and pull back. Family-related comments could unsettle her too. If relatives spoke warmly about family life or asked questions that seemed to assume trust and ease, she would become guarded, hearing in those exchanges something she could not fully explain but did not want to feel.

At home, where she had hoped to feel safest, María remained on guard. She listened for sounds that might mean someone was entering her house, especially doors opening or slamming, and the noise could make her body react before she had time to think. She described herself as constantly tense and ready to react to danger, even when nothing was happening. That alertness was part of her daily routine in a way that had become almost automatic: she would pause when she heard a door, listen carefully, and scan for what the sound meant. Although she was no longer in the relationship in which the abuse occurred, the ordinary setting of her own home still felt like a place where she had to be prepared.

María had worked for years as a pharmacist, a role that had given her a sense of competence, usefulness, and professional identity. In recent years, she has come to feel that she is no longer capable of doing the things that defined her, and this belief has weighed heavily on her. She spoke with sadness about how her world had become smaller and how much of what once felt natural now required effort. She also said she had lost faith in people, life, or a higher power, and that loss was not abstract for her; it was tied to the experience of being harmed by someone she had once expected to trust. On difficult days she called herself weak, not in a fleeting self-critical way but as a settled conclusion about who she is. That judgment sat alongside the shame she felt when remembering the abuse and the sense that her own body still carried the imprint of what happened.

What finally brought María to seek help was the combination of her persistent vigilance at home and the growing weight of living so guardedly. She was tired of listening for danger in her own house, tired of reacting to doors and comments and closeness as if they were warnings, and tired of feeling estranged from the person she had been. At intake, she said she wanted relief, but she also admitted she was frightened that if she stopped being on guard, she would somehow become vulnerable again. At the same time, she hoped that treatment might help her feel less ashamed when the memories came and less alone inside the life she has been trying to manage in silence.
